Chapter 6. Life After Escape—The Weight of the Past.
Freedom—at first, it almost feels like a wide-open sky, doesn’t it? But if you’ve spent years living by someone else’s rules, that new world outside can be just as overwhelming as the one you left behind.
Those first days after leaving the church were a strange mix of relief and anxiety. Suddenly, there was no one watching, no rituals to follow, and no constant surveillance. But there was also no guidebook for what to do next.
Even the simplest things—like choosing what to read, who to call, or how to fill a Sunday—suddenly felt huge. Every choice seemed like a test of this fragile new independence. And those old habits? They didn’t just vanish. The urge to check in or the fear of saying the wrong thing lingered, always close by. The past didn’t just fade away; it stuck to every thought, every conversation.
Some days, the memories came flooding back. All those hours spent in church courses, the whispered warnings about outsiders, the doubts you had to shove aside. It was easy to feel lost. Maybe you even wondered if leaving had been a mistake. That church voice, once so loud, would echo in the background—reminding you of everything you’d given up.
But then, there were these tiny moments of quiet joy. Like taking a walk in the park without having to look over your shoulder. Or calling up an old friend and laughing—really laughing—without fear of who might be listening. The world, which once felt so small, slowly started to open up.
And here’s something important: healing isn’t about forgetting where you came from. It’s about learning to live with the past—finding ways to carry those memories without letting them call the shots.
Most people have no idea how long it takes to unlearn old fears. It’s a slow process, sometimes even painful. But every little step forward? That’s a victory. The past might never let go completely, but it doesn’t have to decide where you go next.
